change_description: Hagia Sophia converted into the city's premier imperial mosque immediately, retaining its name (Ayasofya).
George Scholarios (Gennadios II) appointed Orthodox patriarch on 6 January 1454, continuing the patriarchate under Ottoman authority and, per Oz, encouraging former Christian residents to return.

Forced and incentivized resettlement (surgun) of Muslim, Christian, and Jewish populations from across the empire (Rumelian Jews, Bursa residents moved to Eyup, Serbian/Hungarian/Bulgarian settlers, Morea population in 1459-60); an initial 1453 wave of Anatolian settlers reportedly returned home by autumn, showing the policy needed repeated iterations.
fact_or_interpretation: Fact (policy and specific waves are documented); the demographic 'success' framing is interpretation

change_description: First post-conquest survey (partial) of Istanbul and Galata completed, recording households by quarter.
Waqf (religious endowment) deed for Hagia Sophia drawn up, financing its operation as a mosque complex.
Yedikule Fortress built behind the Byzantine Golden Gate, repurposing part of the old defensive circuit as an Ottoman citadel/treasury.
Strategic relocation of the Ottoman capital from Edirne to Istanbul (per Necipoglu, citing Kritoboulos); popular narratives sometimes date this to 1453 itself.
fact_or_interpretation: Fact (date is contested between scholarly and popular framings)

change_description: Topkapi Palace (the 'New Palace') constructed on the old acropolis; foundation in 1459, completion inscription dated 1478 on the Imperial Gate.
Fatih Mosque complex built on the site of the Byzantine Church of the Holy Apostles; construction initiated 1459, foundation inscription dated 1463-70; complex included eight madrasas.
Major plague outbreak reported (over 600 dead); Oz notes the city nonetheless saw large population growth over the following decade, implying continued in-migration outweighed plague losses.
Tiled Kiosk (Cinili Kosk) completed as part of the palace building programme.
Household census of the Istanbul side records 16,324 households, the first solid quantitative population anchor for the post-conquest city (see population_1477_households.csv).
Fatih complex endowments furnished with shops and other commercial establishments; a gold coin minted from 1477-78.
Ottoman-Venetian peace treaty concluded, restoring commercial ties with a major former opponent; the Venetian painter Gentile Bellini resident at the Ottoman court 1479-81.
Death of Mehmed II (3 May 1481) closes the founding reign of the reconstructed Ottoman capital; the building and resettlement programme he began continued under his successors.

Across roughly three decades the city moved from a depopulated, war-damaged Byzantine capital toward a functioning, endowed, multi-confessional Ottoman capital with a new palace, mosque complex, and administrative registers - though full recovery to the city's peak medieval population took considerably longer (see population_context.csv for later-period estimates).
fact_or_interpretation: Interpretation (synthesis of the fact rows above)
